claims.claim: Axelrod & Hamilton (1981) state TFT is 'evolutionarily stable' iff the continuation probability w is large enough: w >= (T-R)/(T-P) and w >= (T-R)/(R-S). Their stability test is 'cannot be invaded by a rare mutant', checked against ALL D and alternation of D and C.
claims.quote: neither of these two strategies (and hence no strategy at all) can invade TIT FOR TAT if and only if both w ≥ (T - R)/(T - P) and w ≥ (T - R)/(R - S) ... This demonstrates that TIT FOR TAT is evolutionarily stable if and only if the interactions between the individuals have a sufficiently large probability of continuing
claims.source_title: Axelrod & Hamilton, The Evolution of Cooperation, Science 211:1390-1396
claims.notes: OCR'd JSTOR scan on Axelrod's own site; the '≥' sign is OCR'd as '2'. The definition the paper uses is 'cannot be invaded by a rare mutant adopting a different strategy', where invading means doing strictly better. That is weaker than Maynard Smith's ESS second condition, so a neutral mutant such as ALLC is not ruled out. The 'collective stability' wording comes from Axelrod 1981 APSR (see N02).

claims.claim: Axelrod's 1981 APSR paper frames the result as necessary and sufficient conditions for a strategy to be 'collectively stable' and for 'no strategy can do any better than the population average' against TFT. This is a no-strict-improvement (Nash-type) condition, not Maynard Smith's ESS.
claims.quote: (1) the conditions under which no strategy can do any better than the population average if the others are using the reciprocal cooperation strategy of TIT FOR TAT, (2) the necessary and sufficient conditions for a strategy to be collectively stable
claims.source_title: Axelrod, The Emergence of Cooperation among Egoists, APSR 75(2):306-318 (abstract)
claims.notes: Abstract only. The formal definition text from APSR or the 1984 book was not reached. Bendor & Swistak 1995 (N06) is the primary-literature source for 'stable in a weaker sense'.

claims.claim: Boyd & Lorberbaum (1987, Nature) argue that no pure strategy can be evolutionarily stable in the repeated PD, and that this casts doubt on several of Axelrod's conclusions.
claims.quote: In this paper, however, we argue that no pure strategy can be evolutionarily stable in this game. This fact casts doubt on several of Axelrod's conclusions about the evolution of reciprocity.
claims.source_title: Boyd & Lorberbaum, No pure strategy is evolutionarily stable in the repeated Prisoner's Dilemma game, Nature 327:58-59
claims.notes: Opening paragraph from the Nature page. The body was not reached. The often-cited mechanism (TFT is invaded by a mix of e.g. TF2T and STFT when w is large) is NOT verified from primary text. Conditions: no errors, w high enough that many strategies are best replies.

claims.claim: Boyd (1989) showed that if errors always occur with some probability, a pure strategy CAN be evolutionarily stable, provided it is a 'strong perfect equilibrium' against itself. Both ALLD and a modified TFT qualify.
claims.quote: if there is always some probability that individuals will make a mistake, then a pure strategy can be evolutionarily stable provided that it is "strong perfect equilibria" against itself ... I show that both unconditional defection and a modified version of tit-for-tat have this property.
claims.source_title: Boyd, Mistakes allow evolutionary stability in the repeated prisoner's dilemma game, J Theor Biol 136:47-56
claims.notes: Wu & Axelrod 1995 cite Boyd 1989, along with Sugden 1986, as the origin of contrition. The 'modified TFT' is the contrite-style TFT. Plain TFT is not on the list.

claims.claim: Farrell & Ware (1989) extended Boyd & Lorberbaum's result to finite mixtures of strategies.
claims.source_title: Farrell & Ware, Evolutionary stability in the repeated prisoner's dilemma, Theor Pop Biol 36:161-168
claims.notes: Abstract not reachable (Elsevier elided). Secondary descriptions found through search: Bendor & Swistak say Farrell & Ware generalized the result to mixed strategies and conclude ESS is 'too strong'; Linster says any ESS mixture must make every finite history occur with positive probability. Treat as unverified.

claims.claim: Bendor & Swistak (1995, PNAS) reconcile Axelrod-Hamilton with Boyd-Lorberbaum. Under the attainable (weaker) stability concept, the IPD has 'too many' stable strategies, so stability alone does not discriminate. Stable strategies differ in how large an invasion they resist, and TFT-like conditional cooperators are the most robust.
claims.quote: We first show that the IPD has "too many" such strategies, so that being stable does not discriminate among behavioral rules. Stable strategies differ, however, on a property that is crucial for their evolutionary survival--the size of the invasion they can resist. ... Conditionally cooperative strategies such as tit for tat are the most robust.
claims.source_title: Bendor & Swistak, Types of evolutionary stability and the problem of cooperation, PNAS 92:3596-3600
claims.notes: A pro-TFT counterpoint. Its robustness claim is about the noiseless game with a sufficiently long shadow of the future, so it is not a claim about noise.

claims.claim: Selten & Hammerstein (1984, BBS commentary) are cited alongside Boyd & Lorberbaum for the point that TFT is not evolutionarily stable: without noise, ALLC earns the same as TFT and can drift in.
claims.quote: Imagine a mixed population of players using TFT and players using the strategy 'always-cooperate' (ALLC). In the absence of noise, both strategies have the same average payoff. The frequency (=relative abundance) of ALLC can increase by random drift. This means TFT is not evolutionarily stable ( Boyd and Lorberbaum, 1987 ; Selten and Hammerstein, 1984 ).
claims.source_title: Imhof, Fudenberg & Nowak, Tit-for-tat or win-stay, lose-shift? J Theor Biol 247:574-580
claims.notes: Selten & Hammerstein, 'Gaps in Harley's argument on evolutionarily stable learning rules and in the logic of "tit for tat"', BBS 7:115-116. The text itself was NOT reached. The attribution of the 'mistake causes alternating retaliation' argument to S&H specifically is unverified; Nowak 2006 cites S&H (ref 16) for the trembling-hands decline of TFT (see N09).

claims.claim: The echo: if one of two TFT players defects by mistake, the pair falls into alternating C/D. In the infinitely repeated game with noise, TFT vs TFT averages only (R+S+T+P)/4 per round.
claims.quote: If two TFT players interact with each other and one defects by mistake, then the other one will retaliate, which in turn leads to a sequence of alternating moves of cooperation and defection. In the presence of noise, in an infinitely repeated game, the expected payoff per round for TFT versus TFT is only ( R + S + T + P )/4.
claims.source_title: Imhof, Fudenberg & Nowak 2007, J Theor Biol
claims.notes: (R+S+T+P)/4 is the long-run average under any small positive error rate with no discounting (the limit ε→0 of the ergodic average). With T=5,R=3,P=1,S=0 that is 2.25 instead of 3.

claims.claim: Nowak's 2006 Science review calls errors ('trembling hands' or 'fuzzy minds') the 'Achilles heel' of TFT, citing Fudenberg & Maskin 1990 and Selten & Hammerstein 1984. It describes a succession: TFT replaced by GTFT, then by WSLS. TFT is a catalyst where nearly everyone defects, but WSLS better maintains cooperation once it is established.
claims.quote: if there are erroneous moves, caused by 'trembling hands' or 'fuzzy minds', then the performance of tit-for-tat declines ( 15 , 16 ). Tit-for-tat cannot correct mistakes, because an accidental defection leads to a long sequence of retaliation. ... Tit-for-tat is an efficient catalyst of cooperation in a society where nearly everybody is a defector, but once cooperation is established win-stay, lose-shift is better able to maintain it.
claims.source_title: Nowak, Five rules for the evolution of cooperation, Science 314:1560-1563 (author manuscript)
claims.notes: Refs 15 = Fudenberg & Maskin AER 1990; 16 = Selten & Hammerstein BBS 1984; 17 = Nowak & Sigmund 1992; 18 = Nowak & Sigmund 1993.

claims.claim: Molander (1985): TFT's performance in the iterated PD deteriorates drastically at arbitrarily low noise levels. Adding some unconditional generosity remedies this without exposure to exploitation.
claims.quote: The tit-for-tat strategy in iterated prisoners' dilemma games is examined in the presence of disturbances. It is shown that performance deteriorates drastically at arbitrarily low noise levels. The situation may be remedied by introducing some unconditional generosity. This may be done without exposing oneself to the risk of exploitation by the other party.
claims.source_title: Molander, The Optimal Level of Generosity in a Selfish, Uncertain Environment, JCR 29(4):611-618
claims.notes: Abstract only; the full text (SAGE) was not reached. Molander's own formula for the optimal generosity level was NOT seen in primary text (see N12 for the formula as stated by Hilbe et al. 2018, who cite Molander for it).

claims.claim: As reported by Wu & Axelrod, Molander showed that with any amount of noise, two TFT players in the long run average the same payoffs as two RANDOM players.
claims.quote: Molander (1985) has shown that in the presence of any amount of noise, two Tit for Tat (TFT) players will in the long run average the same payoffs as two interacting RANDOM players.
claims.source_title: Wu & Axelrod, How to Cope with Noise in the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (author version, July 1994), JCR 39:183-189
claims.notes: Verbatim from Wu & Axelrod, but secondhand about Molander's result. This is consistent with N08: the (R+S+T+P)/4 average equals the payoff of two 50/50 RANDOM players. It holds in the long-run, undiscounted limit.

claims.claim: Generosity bound: in the undiscounted (δ=1) game, a reactive strategy (p,q) is a 'partner' iff p=1 and q < q*, where q* = min{1-(T-R)/(R-S), (R-P)/(T-P)}. GTFT's forgiveness q must be large enough to avoid vendettas but low enough to give ALLD no selective advantage (citing Molander 1985).
claims.quote: Without discounting, δ = 1, a reactive strategy is a partner if and only if p = 1 and q < q ∗ with q ∗ = min{1−(T −R)/(R−S), (R−P )/(T −P )}.
claims.source_title: Hilbe, Chatterjee & Nowak, Partners and rivals in direct reciprocity, Nat Hum Behav 2:469-477 (submitted version, Box 2)
claims.notes: Submitted version, not the typeset text. Main text: 'The probability q can be chosen sufficiently large to avoid costly vendettas after an error, but low enough to give ALLD no selective advantage [41=Molander]'. With T=5,R=3,P=1,S=0: q* = min(1/3, 1/2) = 1/3. In the donation game (T=b,R=b-c,P=0,S=-c) both terms equal 1-c/b, matching Nowak 2006 (N13). A Király EGT lecture (egt04.pdf) gives the same formula as 'q_opt' for Nowak & Sigmund 1992.

claims.claim: In Nowak's 2006 donation-game framing, GTFT cooperates whenever you cooperate and sometimes cooperates after you defect, with probability 1 - c/b.
claims.quote: generous-tit-for-tat ( 17 ), a strategy which cooperates whenever you cooperate, but sometimes cooperates although you have defected (with probability 1 − c/b ). Natural selection can promote forgiveness.
claims.source_title: Nowak 2006, Science
claims.notes: Ref 17 = Nowak & Sigmund 1992. The b/c parameterization is the donation-game special case of N12.

claims.claim: Nowak & Sigmund (1992, Nature): in heterogeneous, error-prone populations, a small fraction of TFT is essential for reciprocation to emerge, but it only paves the way for a more generous strategy. TFT is 'the pivot, rather than the aim'.
claims.quote: We find that a small fraction of TFT players is essential for the emergence of reciprocation in a heterogeneous population, but only paves the way for a more generous strategy. TFT is the pivot, rather than the aim, of an evolution towards cooperation.
claims.source_title: Nowak & Sigmund, Tit for tat in heterogeneous populations, Nature 355:250-253
claims.notes: Opening paragraph only. Setup (secondhand): reactive strategies (p,q) with stochasticity. The evolved generosity q≈1/3 under standard payoffs is reported by Grim (1996, philarchive GRISAG) and is consistent with N12. The value is NOT verified from the 1992 body text.

claims.claim: Evolutionary trajectories among reactive strategies often run ALLD → TFT → GTFT.
claims.quote: Although reactive strategies contain both ALLD and TFT, stochastic simulations typically favor a more lenient strategy. Evolutionary trajectories often lead from ALLD to TFT and from there to Generous Tit for Tat (GTFT) 42 .
claims.source_title: Hilbe, Chatterjee & Nowak 2018 (submitted version)
claims.notes: Ref 42 = Nowak & Sigmund 1992. This holds within the reactive (memory-1 on the opponent only) strategy space.

claims.claim: Nowak & Sigmund (1993, Nature): extended evolutionary simulations of heterogeneous ensembles of probabilistic strategies with mutation and selection found Pavlov (win-stay, lose-shift) unexpectedly successful. Its two advantages over TFT are correcting occasional mistakes and exploiting unconditional cooperators. The second prevents ALLC drift, which would invite defectors.
claims.quote: Pavlov's success is based on two important advantages over tit-for-tat: it can correct occasional mistakes and exploit unconditional cooperators. This second feature prevents Pavlov populations from being undermined by unconditional cooperators, which in turn invite defectors. Pavlov seems to be more robust than tit-for-tat
claims.source_title: Nowak & Sigmund, A strategy of win-stay, lose-shift that outperforms tit-for-tat in the Prisoner's Dilemma game, Nature 364:56-58
claims.notes: The abstract hedges with 'seems to be more robust'. Simulation specifics (memory-one strategies (p1..p4), error rate, payoffs, run counts) were NOT read from primary text; the body is paywalled. Wu & Axelrod describe it as 'a simulated evolutionary process that included noise, but allowed strategies with memory of only the preceding move'.

claims.claim: Pavlov/WSLS is vulnerable to ALLD: after mutual defection it cooperates, so ALLD can alternate T and P. Wu & Axelrod give the condition: always-defect beats Pavlov at low noise if T + wP > R + wR, i.e. w < (T-R)/(R-P). With T=5,R=3,P=1,S=0 and any w<1, it pays to always defect against Pavlov.
claims.quote: It pays to always defect when playing with Pavlov at low levels of noise if alternating T and P is better than always getting R. With standard notation, this is true when T+wP > R+wR or w < (T-R)/(R-P). Thus, with the standard payoffs of T=5, R=3, P=1, S=0, and any w < 1, it pays to always defect when playing with Pavlov.
claims.source_title: Wu & Axelrod 1995 (author version), footnote 3
claims.notes: Hilbe 2018 has the matching condition: 'WSLS is a partner strategy if δ > (T−R)/(R−P) and δ > (T−R)/(T−S), which is a sharper condition' than TFT's δ > (T−R)/(T−P), δ > (T−R)/(R−S). As δ→1 this requires 2R > T+P, which fails at the boundary for the 5/3/1/0 payoffs. Imhof 2007: 'WSLS is exploited by ALLD in every second round whereas TFT is not.'

claims.claim: Wu & Axelrod (1995) reran Axelrod's second-round environment of 63 rules (average interaction length 151 moves) with 1% noise and added GTFT (cooperates 10% of the time it would otherwise defect), Contrite TFT, Pavlov and Generous Pavlov. GTFT scored higher than any of the 63 original rules. CTFT beat all but five. Pavlov ranked below 55 of the 63 and GPavlov below 48.
claims.quote: To this environment we add 1% noise, meaning that for each intended choice there is a 1% chance that the opposite choice will actually be implemented. ... The highest score is attained by GTFT which actually does better than any of the 63 rules submitted. CTFT also does very well, better than all but five of the 63 rules. Pavlov does poorly, ranking below 55 of the 63 rules. Adding generosity to Pavlov helps only a little: GPavlov ranks below 48 of the 63 rules.
claims.source_title: Wu & Axelrod 1995 (author version)
claims.notes: Scores are averaged over 20 replications. GTFT's generosity here is 10%, not the q*=1/3 bound. The noise sweep (0.1% to 10%) found GTFT and CTFT do well at all levels; GTFT is slightly better at low noise, CTFT slightly better when noise > 1%. The paper does not state how plain TFT ranked in the noisy rerun.

claims.claim: In Wu & Axelrod's ecological simulation (67 rules, 1% noise, 2000 generations), Contrite TFT became the leader by generation 1000 and reached 97% of the population by generation 2000. GTFT had early success, then faded. Both Pavlov versions fell below one part in a million by about generation 100.
claims.quote: By generation 1000, CTFT was the leader. It continued to grow, eventually becoming 97% of the population at generation 2000. GTFT had some early success, but then faded. Both versions of Pavlov declined to less than one part in a million as early as the hundred generation. The clear winner in this ecological simulation with noise was CTFT.
claims.source_title: Wu & Axelrod 1995 (author version)
claims.notes: Conclusion: GTFT is best against populations not adapted to noise. CTFT is better once others have adapted, because contrition corrects only one's own errors (CTFT vs TFT still echoes after TFT's error). 'Pavlov is not robust'. This contradicts the Nowak-Sigmund 1993 headline; the difference is in environment (Axelrod's 63 rules vs a memory-one ensemble) and payoffs (5/3/1/0, where ALLD exploits Pavlov).

claims.claim: Wu & Axelrod's abstract summarizes the three findings: GTFT is highly effective when the players it meets have not adapted to noise; CTFT is even more effective if they have; Pavlov is not robust.
claims.quote: (1) a generous version of tit-for-tat is a highly effective strategy when the players it meets have not adapted to noise; (2) if the other players have adapted to noise, a contrite version of tit-for-tat is even more effective at quickly restoring mutual cooperation without the risk of exploitation; and (3) Pavlov is not robust.
claims.source_title: Wu & Axelrod, JCR 39(1):183-189 (abstract)
claims.notes: In his 2001 Routledge encyclopedia entry Axelrod restates that TFT 'is overly sensitive to misunderstanding or misimplementation' and that this can be corrected by generosity or contrition (public.websites.umich.edu/~axe/research/TitForTat.pdf).

claims.claim: Kraines & Kraines (1989) introduced the name 'Pavlov' for a conditioned-response learner in the extended-play PD. WSLS is also known as Pavlov (Kraines & Kraines 1989, 1995) and as 'perfect tit-for-tat'.
claims.quote: Our Pavlov learns by conditioned response, through rewards and punishments, to cooperate or defect.
claims.source_title: Kraines & Kraines, Pavlov and the prisoner's dilemma, Theory and Decision 26(1):47-79 (abstract via Duke Scholars)
claims.notes: Only the first abstract sentence was captured verbatim, through a fetch tool, not a raw page. Imhof 2007: 'WSLS is also known as Pavlov ( Kraines and Kraines, 1989 , 1995 )'; 'Another name for WSLS is "perfect tit-for-tat;" ... the rule is a symmetric subgame-perfect equilibrium, while TFT is typically not.' The Kraines Pavlov is a learning automaton with graded probabilities, not identical to deterministic WSLS (1,0,0,1).

claims.claim: Fudenberg & Maskin (1990) showed WSLS is evolutionarily stable in the set of finite-complexity strategies in repeated games with errors, while TFT is not.
claims.quote: Fudenberg and Maskin (1990) considered a concept of evolutionary stability for repeated games with errors and showed that WSLS is, in this sense, evolutionarily stable in the set of strategies of finite complexity, while TFT is not.
claims.source_title: Imhof, Fudenberg & Nowak 2007 (describing Fudenberg & Maskin, AER 80:274-279)
claims.notes: This is Fudenberg (a coauthor) describing his own 1990 result. The AER paper was not reached.

claims.claim: Folk theorem (as stated in a review): for a sufficiently large continuation probability δ, any feasible payoff pair in which both players get at least P can arise in equilibrium. Theory does not single out TFT, and in evolving populations none of these equilibria is evolutionarily stable without mistakes, because of neutral stepping-stone invasions (TFT→ALLC→ALLD; ALLD→STFT→...).
claims.quote: The folk theorem 21,22 guarantees that any feasible average payoff can arise in equilibrium, provided that players get at least the mutual defection payoff P (Fig. 1c). On the other hand, in evolving populations none of those equilibria are evolutionarily stable 23–26 . ... Such neutral, stepping-stone invasions are always possible 27,28 , unless there is a positive probability of mistakes 29,30 .
claims.source_title: Hilbe, Chatterjee & Nowak 2018 (submitted version)
claims.notes: Refs 21-22 = Friedman 1971, Aumann 1981; 23-26 = Maynard Smith 1982, Selten & Hammerstein 1984, Boyd & Lorberbaum 1987, Bendor & Swistak; 29-30 = Boyd 1989, Fudenberg & Maskin 1990. The Fig. 1 caption reads 'for sufficiently large δ, all payoff pairs in which both players get at least P can arise in equilibrium'. Axelrod & Hamilton 1981 already note 'when w is sufficiently great, there is no single best strategy regardless of the behavior of the others'.

claims.claim: Nowak (2006): direct reciprocity can only lead to cooperation if the probability w of another encounter exceeds c/b. In the TFT-vs-ALLD matrix, the thresholds are b/c > 1/w (ESS), b/c > (2-w)/w (risk-dominance) and b/c > (3-2w)/w (advantageous).
claims.quote: Direct reciprocity can only lead to the evolution of cooperation if the probability, w , of another encounter between the same two individuals exceeds the cost-to-benefit ratio of the altruistic act: w > c / b .
claims.source_title: Nowak 2006, Science (author manuscript)
claims.notes: The thresholds come from Table 1 (PMC text extraction; the fractions were flattened). The rule assumes cooperators use TFT and defectors ALLD, with no errors. It is a 'simple rule', not a general characterization.

claims.claim: Imhof, Fudenberg & Nowak (2005, PNAS): with only ALLD, ALLC and TFT under mutation-selection in finite populations, the population cycles ALLD → TFT → ALLC → ALLD, although ALLD is the only strict Nash equilibrium. The time average can be concentrated entirely on TFT.
claims.quote: Despite ALLD being the only strict Nash equilibrium, we observe evolutionary oscillations among all three strategies. The population cycles from ALLD to TFT to ALLC and back to ALLD. Most surprisingly, the time average of these oscillations can be entirely concentrated on TFT.
claims.source_title: Imhof, Fudenberg & Nowak, Evolutionary cycles of cooperation and defection, PNAS 102:10797-10800
claims.notes: This is a finite-population stochastic model without errors in the base model. It is a pro-TFT result conditional on the strategy set {ALLD, ALLC, TFT}.

claims.claim: Imhof, Fudenberg & Nowak (2007): with errors, in finite populations (limits u→0, N→∞), among ALLD, ALLC, TFT and WSLS, either ALLD is selected (benefit below a critical value) or WSLS is selected (above it). TFT is never selected but lowers the threshold for WSLS. In the donation game the threshold is b/c > 3 for weak selection without TFT and drops to 2 with TFT present.
claims.quote: If instead of TFT, WSLS competes with ALLC and ALLD, then WSLS is selected, provided the benefit-to-cost ratio, b / c , is sufficiently large. The critical value is 3 in the limit of weak selection. d) Similar behavior as in c) is observed if TFT is added, but the critical value is now lowered to 2 for any intensity of selection.
claims.source_title: Imhof, Fudenberg & Nowak, Tit-for-tat or win-stay, lose-shift? J Theor Biol 247:574-580
claims.notes: Abstract: 'TFT is never selected in this evolutionary process, but lowers the selection threshold for WSLS.' Body: 'TFT is a catalyst for the emergence of cooperation, but is not the target of evolution.' Assumptions: infinitely repeated PD, error probability ε small, R > (T+S)/2. In the ALLD+TFT+ALLC system with noise, the equilibrium distribution is entirely centred on ALLD. For stronger selection the WSLS-vs-ALLD threshold is somewhat above 3.

claims.claim: Hilbe et al. 2018: WSLS is the only memory-1 strategy that is mutually cooperative, retaliating and error-correcting. It evolves in a wide range of scenarios provided mutual cooperation is sufficiently profitable and the game is iterated for enough rounds. The review's larger frame: successful strategies are either 'partners' or 'rivals'; partners are favoured by large populations and stable relationships, rivals by small populations and few rounds.
claims.quote: WSLS is the only memory-1 strategy that satisfies three simple principles 48 : It is mutually cooperative, retaliating, and error-correcting. ... Due to these principles, WSLS evolves in a wide range of scenarios, provided that mutual cooperation is sufficiently profitable and that the game is iterated for a sufficient number of rounds
claims.source_title: Hilbe, Chatterjee & Nowak 2018 (submitted version); abstract via PubMed 31097794
claims.notes: PubMed abstract: 'Whereas small population sizes and a limited number of rounds favour rivalry, partner strategies are selected when populations are large and relationships stable.' A 2018 publisher correction fixed a missing arrow in Fig. 4 only.

claims.claim: Nowak & Sigmund (1993, PNAS): populations of simple memory-one strategies can show persistent periodic or chaotic oscillations in cooperation. Adding GTFT greatly increases the overall level of cooperation and can lead to long periods of steady cooperation.
claims.quote: Adding "generous tit-for-tat" greatly increases the overall level of cooperation and can lead to long periods of steady cooperation.
claims.source_title: Nowak & Sigmund, Chaos and the evolution of cooperation, PNAS 90:5091-5094
claims.notes: Supports the 'no final winner / cycles' picture.

claims.claim: Human experiments (Wedekind & Milinski 1996) suggest the Pavlov-vs-GTFT ranking depends on game format. Theory predicts Pavlov wins only in the simultaneous game. In humans about 70% played Pavlov-like and 30% GTFT-like; Pavlovian players did better in simultaneous play and GTFT-like players in alternating play.
claims.quote: According to recent developments of theory the last champion strategy of "win--stay, lose--shift" ("Pavlov") is the winner only if the players act simultaneously.
claims.source_title: Wedekind & Milinski, Human cooperation in the simultaneous and the alternating Prisoner's Dilemma: Pavlov versus Generous Tit-for-Tat, PNAS 93:2686-2689
claims.notes: This is a format condition on the WSLS result: it rests on Nowak & Sigmund 1994 (JTB) for the alternating PD. That 1994 paper was not reached.

claims.claim: Knight et al. (2025 preprint) rebuilt Axelrod's second tournament from the surviving Fortran code and reproduced TFT's win. With 1% noise the rankings reshuffle substantially and mean cooperation falls from 0.75 to 0.65. The noisy winner cooperates at 0.61, while TFT cooperates at 0.70; k42r, ranked 10th, outperforms TFT. The authors call the original tournament 'especially favorable to TFT'.
claims.quote: The mean cooperation rate declines from 0.75 (noiseless) to 0.65 under noise (Figure 6c). Correspondingly, the new winning strategy in this setting cooperates at 0.61, slightly below the noisy-tournament mean, whereas TFT cooperates at 0.70, above the mean.
claims.source_title: Knight, Campbell, Harper, Gaffney, Glynatsi, Reviving, reproducing, and revisiting Axelrod's second tournament (arXiv)
claims.notes: Preprint, not peer-reviewed at time of reading. TFT's exact rank under noise is not stated in the extracted text. This is a modern counterpart to Wu & Axelrod's N18 and may overlap with a 'reproduction' research line.

open_questions: Boyd & Lorberbaum 1987 body text: the exact invasion construction (which strategy pair invades TFT, and under what w) was not reached. Avoid asserting 'TF2T + STFT' without the primary text.

Selten & Hammerstein 1984 BBS commentary text was not reached. It is unverified whether they made the noise/echo argument or the neutral-drift/non-ESS argument (secondary sources cite them for non-ESS).

Molander 1985 full text: his own optimal-generosity formula and the payoffs/discounting he assumed. The q* = min{1-(T-R)/(R-S),(R-P)/(T-P)} formula is verified only from Hilbe et al. 2018, which cites Molander for it, and from a lecture slide that attributes it to Nowak & Sigmund 1992.
Nowak & Sigmund 1992 body: the reported evolved q (≈1/3 per Grim 1996, secondhand), payoffs, and error handling.

Nowak & Sigmund 1993 body: strategy space (memory-one p1..p4), error rate (one secondary source says 1%; unverified), payoff values, number of runs, and whether they state the R > (T+P)/2 condition for Pavlov resisting ALLD.
Farrell & Ware 1989 abstract and exact theorem (finite mixtures) — only secondhand descriptions were seen.
Axelrod's formal definition of 'collectively stable' (APSR 1981 / 1984 book), to quote precisely that it requires only that no mutant does strictly better (Nash), i.e. weaker than ESS.
Fudenberg & Maskin 1990 AER result (WSLS-type ESS under errors) — only Fudenberg's coauthored description was seen.
Wu & Axelrod 1995: plain TFT's rank in the 1%-noise rerun is not given in the text (Fig. 1 is an image).
